sections.title: Permanent Impermanence
sections.summary: One light in an underpass, and nobody stops. I turn the everyday structure of a public space into an artwork. It feels like it's always been there, but now people want to stay.
sections.describe:
I am Gill
I am James
I am an artist
a Cree voice rising

I wrote those lines for my site and it's still where I start. Picture an underpass in Vancouver at dusk. One light, concrete, and nobody stops. Come back later. The same light falls on wood shaped by hand and on plants that belong here. Someone sits. Then someone else.

In my words: "When we are done it should feel like it was always there, but be a space people want to spend time in. A hub, a gathering place. It can be activated or left to rest"

I make infrastructure as art, through an ethnobotanical lens. Seats, edges, light and plants, rooted in culture and made for people. The art has a job in the space, like the lighting does, and it's still art.

I add “invisible” elements too. By invisible I mean light, framing and composition in 3D space, the things that affect how folks feel and pull on the subconscious.

Joshua Ngenda and I wrote it into Spirit Eye: "imagining essential infrastructure as art" and the "basic human need for light & nature".

It's more than a stage. In my words, "imagining and considering how both the seer and the seen are considered." The audience gets places to settle, at different heights.

The living part is art too. It can sit inside what's already growing, or become a new forest garden, made for what it will be in 100, 300 and 1,000 years. In my words, "using existing public space that through my treatment become a space to be." The Host Nations and plant knowledge keepers guide what grows here. Learning from them is part of the work.

I'm looking for an underused spot in Vancouver with good bones. Some light already there, natural levels, a place to sit and watch. I'll respect what's there and leave it improved, not overpowered. [GILL TO CONFIRM: any site or landowner already in talks.]

The form stays open. A bench, a frame, a carving. The site and the making decide. My vision, philosophy and guiding principles hold the whole way through.

I wrote this on 9 November:

"Even set it up like a “stage” “set” elements to transform space but transferable. Understand? Permanent impermanence"

The set can move. The living part stays and grows.

I wrote: “We will be mounting a piece to open the "space" probably going to use alternate name for that music project. Run it like mounting a theatre run but with an album, live.” That opens the space, under [PROJECT NAME TBC].

I'm Cree-Métis, a status member of Norway House Cree Nation, Two-Spirit (he/him), and I live in Vancouver.

The making:
- Find the site and sort out permissions and insurance.
- Study the light there, day and night.
- Plan the planting with the right people. [GILL TO CONFIRM: who, and how much planting.]
- Mill my own wood and make test pieces.
- Build and install. A licensed electrician does any wiring. [GILL TO CONFIRM: power at the site.]
- Document it all on my own camera.

I have my tools and a workspace, and I may rent a studio for bigger builds. [GILL TO CONFIRM: studio rental.]

Sound and film projection are a separate Indigenous Screen Office application.
sections.why:
My grandfather, Jack Taylor, was taken from Norway House Cree Nation as a child. His family was made to set aside being Cree so they could pass as white, and that carried a deep shame. Jack found his way back to who he was through art. After he retired from the police force, he went to art school and became a fine artist. He worked in pencil and graphite, watercolour and collage, and made masks that looked almost like carved wood. He invented and built many of his own tools, and he often photographed a scene before he painted it.

I was very close to him, and I spent a lot of time in his studio. That's where I learned that making things with your hands can be a way of holding on to who you are. Our family never went back to Norway House, and I won't claim a closeness to community I haven't earned. But I've always felt that something of it stayed with us, and I saw it in him: in the way he worked, and in how he made what he needed.

Some of his work is still here. This project picks up a thread he left me. His masks reached toward carved wood, and I'm carving the wood itself, in yellow cedar. He worked from photographs, and I work through a camera. He made his own tools, and I design and make objects. This piece is how I carry his line forward, and how I take the step he never got to take: going back to Norway House, if I'm welcomed.

All my relations,
in all my creations
sections.impact:
Fine art and music
are rivers I swim, a daily drift
a lifelong hum

I've worked in film, objects, space, light and sound most of my life. This is my first public artwork at full scale, and it draws on all of it. It moves my work from objects into places. It's not a picture on a wall.

When it's done there's a finished, documented place-work, and a way of working I can bring to public art calls and commissions. It opens with a live album, run like a theatre run, under [PROJECT NAME TBC]. What stays behind, in my words: "Human centred art as infracture, ecosytem where possible" I've already started on this. My public art concept Spirit Eye of skwácháýs, co-created with Joshua Ngenda, was recognized with Best Public Art Concept and Council's Choice within the BIDC Public Art Intensive.

It's for whoever walks by, and for the Indigenous community here. [GILL TO CONFIRM: any community group or partner to name.] For me it's a way back toward Norway House through the work, the way Jack found his way back through art. Someone sits. Then someone else. [GILL TO CONFIRM: whether to name any Norway House step here, such as sending the documentation to the Nation if welcomed.]
sections.capacity:
I'm an artist. I'm hands on and I finish what I make. Years ago I wrote that I have "an inate sense of story and an uncanny fluency in visual language," and that's still true, whether I'm working with light or wood.

- Cinematography: a CSC Cinematography Award and the Leo Award for Best Cinematography in a Short Drama (2015), both for One With the Devil, and Leo cinematography nominations for Arc (2015) and Backward Fall (2014). I also produced Backward Fall.
- Directing and producing: co-director with Jett Pace, cinematographer and producer on Old Man Canyon's "Back to the Start".
- Public art: Spirit Eye of skwácháýs, co-created with Joshua Ngenda in the BIDC Public Art Intensive (June 2025), recognized with Best Public Art Concept and Council's Choice within the BIDC Public Art Intensive.
- Objects and carving: I design and make carved wooden pieces, including hand-carved paddles, with my own gouges and power carving tools.
- Material: I mill my own dimensional yellow cedar.
- Land: trail stewardship keeps me outside working with my hands, in all weather. [GILL TO CONFIRM: wording.]
- Sound: I make music as Mothers Moniker.
- Education: film production at UBC (2014), and design and advertising at OCAD. [GILL TO CONFIRM: education wording.]

My work lives in light, framing and composition in 3D space, how they affect the way folks feel and pull on the subconscious. I carry that into wood, sound and the places I make. I make big ideas happen. I've run large, complex projects for over a decade, with crews, budgets and tight timelines. My principles come from years of building. Start simple and familiar. Keep it quiet, local and human. Respect the original. Make it feel like it was always there. I enjoy self directed creation, and this project is sized for one maker, with a helper for safety on heavy lifts.
sections.timeline:
1 Apr 2027 to 31 Jan 2028 (10 months).

Apr to Jun 2027: look at sites. Underused plazas, lit underpasses and park edges, with waterfront as a backup. Study the light, day and night. Mill wood, make test pieces, and start the planting plan with the right people.

Jul to Aug 2027: confirm the site and permissions. Make the pieces and line up the plants. Rent a studio if I need one.

Sep to Oct 2027: install. A helper on heavy days, and a licensed electrician for any wiring.

Nov 2027: the opening. A live album, run like a theatre run, under [PROJECT NAME TBC]. [GILL TO CONFIRM: exact site, dates, number of shows, whether the album is new, whether the run is ticketed or free, and whether this opening is the CKS public sharing.]

Dec 2027 to Jan 2028: finish the documentation and the final report. Hand care of the living part to the site partner. [GILL TO CONFIRM: who.]
sections.protocol: This comes from my own practice and my own family. I'm not using traditional knowledge, ceremony or cultural forms I haven't been given the right to use. I'm a Cree-Métis guest on this coast, and I won't borrow the Host Nations' crests, forms or stories. Plants carry knowledge, so I'll ask first [GILL TO CONFIRM: which Host Nation contacts or Elders to approach first], pay honoraria, follow their lead, and name people only if they say yes. Any step toward Norway House follows the Nation's process.
sections.collaborators: I'm making this on my own. I'll pay a helper for heavy lifting, for safety only, and a licensed electrician for any wiring. [GILL TO CONFIRM: whether the helper can be an Indigenous maker.] Plant knowledge keepers will be paid, and named only if they agree.
